source: Kolling, Behrens, Mars, Rushworth (2012) Neural mechanisms of foraging
finding: Humans switched between comparing fixed options (engage) and foraging (search for a better set). ACC tracked the average value of the search environment and search cost. vmPFC tracked the chosen option's value.
numbers: fMRI; t(17) reported, so about 18 participants (inferred, N not stated in page text). ACC search-value slope steeper on search than engage trials, t(17)=-2.54, p=0.021. Stimuli from 12 learned values; search cost high/mid/low.
quote: Engaging was promoted by search costs and encounter values but retarded by all components of search values
limits: N inferred. Stats mostly in figures and supplement. Later work (a08) says the ACC effect may be choice difficulty.
agent_relevance: S6 trigger idea: compare the value of searching elsewhere (environment average) with the current option, not with the best alternative alone.

source: Kolling et al. (2012) behavioural bias: forage readiness
finding: People needed more objective value gain to search than to engage. The authors call this a bias against searching.
numbers: Effect is qualitative in the page text; exact bias size not given.
limits: Page text lacks the equations (SOM Eq 2-4).
agent_relevance: Real deciders under-switch. A scaffold trigger should be a hard rule in code, not left to the model's feeling of being stuck.

source: Kolling et al. (2012) ventral striatum and ACC coupling
finding: Ventral striatum showed post-search prediction-error-like responses and scaled with search cost. ACC coupled more with left ventral striatum as search cost rose.
numbers: People who searched less had larger peak striatal responses; cost response scaled with how much cost deterred searching.
limits: Correlational fMRI.
agent_relevance: Search cost should be an explicit input to the leave rule (cost of switching operators).

source: Hayden, Pearson, Platt (2011) Neuronal basis of sequential foraging decisions in a patchy environment
finding: Macaque dACC neurons rose in firing as time in patch increased and reached a fixed threshold at the moment of leaving. Longer travel time lowered the response gain and raised the threshold.
numbers: 2 monkeys, 102 dACC neurons (49 with positive slope). Reward started 306 ul, fell about 19 ul per stay. Travel 0.5-10.5 s. Residence time rose with travel time, beta=1.247, P<0.0001, 2834 leaves. Rise slopes by earliness quartile 0.71, 0.52, 0.44, 0.39. Gain beta=-0.033; threshold beta=0.92 (n=49).
quote: These modulations more closely matched behavioral decisions than any single task variable.
limits: Two animals. Focal analysis on 49 selected neurons. Earliness effect on threshold significant in only 6 of 49 neurons. Variable could equally encode negative value of staying.
agent_relevance: A leave decision can be framed as an accumulator hitting a threshold, with the threshold set by the cost of the next source. Matches code-fired S6 triggers.

source: Hayden et al. (2011) behaviour versus MVT
finding: Monkeys followed the marginal value theorem qualitatively but stayed about 2.2 s longer than predicted. MVT beat a delay-discounting model.
numbers: 97.2% of reward of the best-fit rate-maximising strategy. Overstay about 2.2 s (P<0.01). Likelihood ratio MVT over discounting about 1.31e52. Handling-time control: residence fell with handling time, beta about -3.71.
limits: Virtual task, no physical effort. Overstaying is the first sign of the later overharvesting literature.
agent_relevance: Expect a small bias to stay too long. Set the leave threshold slightly below the observed average, or force the check by code.

source: Constantino and Daw (2015) Learning the opportunity cost of time in a patch-foraging task
finding: Humans changed their leave threshold with travel time and depletion rate. A model that learns the environment's average reward rate (MVT threshold learning) beat temporal-difference learning.
numbers: 52 recruited, 47 analysed (Exp1A 11, 1B 10, Exp2 26). Overharvesting in 3 of 4 Exp2 conditions (t<3.6, p<.002). Earnings about 9-10% below optimal. Best constant-hazard policy 25-33% below optimal. Bayesian model selection MVT vs TD: Exp1 exp.freq 0.83, exceedance 0.999; Exp2 0.85 / 0.999. MVT vs R-learning 0.87 and 0.93.
quote: Trial-by-trial decisions were better explained by the MVT threshold learning rule.
limits: Small N per experiment. Fitted parameters not in the text read. Overharvesting intercepts remained for MVT (t20=-4.87 Exp1; -7.48 Exp2) and vanished with a risk-sensitivity parameter (p=.2, .10).
agent_relevance: Direct support for an average-yield rule: learn the running mean yield per unit time and leave when instantaneous yield falls below it. Cost of switching is part of that mean.

source: Constantino and Daw (2015) adaptation across environments
finding: Thresholds fell in poorer environments (longer travel, steeper depletion), as MVT says.
numbers: Exp1 travel t10=5.7, p<.001; depletion t9=5.1, p<.001. Exp2 depletion F(1,25)=82, travel F(1,25)=42.1, both p<.001. Only long-travel Exp1 showed overharvesting (t9=-2.3, p=.045).
limits: Overharvest strength depends on condition.
agent_relevance: The threshold should move with the richness of the whole task set, not stay fixed.

source: Shenhav, Straccia, Cohen, Botvinick (2014) ACC engagement in a foraging context reflects choice difficulty, not foraging value
finding: Replicated the Kolling task and found the dACC effect follows choice difficulty. When difficulty and foraging value were decoupled, difficulty predicted dACC and foraging value did not.
numbers: Exp1 N=15: difficulty and value correlated rho=0.80. Exp2 N=14: rho=0.07. Joint model: difficulty t(13)=2.8, p=0.014; foraging value t(13)=0.47, p=0.64. Difficulty larger, paired t(13)=2.2, p=0.046.
quote: dACC responds to foraging value only to the extent that it offers a proxy for choice difficulty
limits: Boundary condition for the neural claim only. Behavioural MVT results are not refuted. Small N.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent on the claim that one brain area computes foraging value. Use the behavioural rule only.

source: Shenhav et al. (2014) indifference point shifted from zero
finding: People did not treat foraging value of zero as the indifference point. Choices were biased toward engaging, as in Kolling.
numbers: Exp1 indifference at RVforage=1.65 (SE 0.26, t14=6.5, p=1.4e-5). Exp2 M=5.0 (SE 1.3, t13=3.9, p=0.0018). Drift diffusion fit.
limits: Kolling's difficulty measure assumed zero indifference; this changes the neural reading.
agent_relevance: Confirms the bias against leaving; add margin to leave rules.

source: Kane et al. (2022) Rat ACC continuously signals decision variables in a patch foraging task
finding: A leaky competing accumulator model with fast (local) and slow (global) reward-rate integrators matched rat ACC activity. ACC inactivation changed trial counts and response times but rats still followed the MVT rule.
numbers: 22 male rats (11 recording, 11 cannulas). 148 ACC units. Trials per patch rose with starting reward, beta=2.294. Inactivation: more trials beta=2.397, RT beta=0.669; only non-decision time changed among LCA parameters (t10=-9.287, p<.001). Patches starting at 30-60 ul were left at a lower reward rate than MVT.
quote: ACC inactivation had a profound effect on rats' foraging decisions and response times
limits: Parameter count reported inconsistently (9 vs 13). Poor patches deviate from MVT. Travel fixed at 10 s.
agent_relevance: Two rates: a fast local yield and a slow average yield. Leave when local falls below global. A direct model of S6.

source: Blanchard and Hayden (2015) Monkeys are more patient in a foraging task than in a standard intertemporal choice task
finding: Four monkeys waited longer in a patch-leaving task than a standard intertemporal choice task predicts. Foraging theory predicted behaviour better than discount rates from the choice task.
numbers: 4 rhesus monkeys. ITC discount k: B 0.768, C 0.426, H 0.496, J 0.380 per s. All left earlier than the ITC model said, P<0.0001 (as stated in the page summary). After outlier exclusion B, H, J overstayed (index -0.116, -0.189, -0.093). Daily discount vs leaving time correlations r -0.219, 0.233, -0.299, 0.236, none significant.
quote: Monkeys were significantly more patient in the foraging task than in the intertemporal choice task.
limits: Four animals. Result is about time preference.
agent_relevance: A rule written as a rate comparison (foraging) behaves more sensibly than a discounting rule.

source: Harhen and Bornstein (2023) Overharvesting in human patch foraging reflects rational structure learning and adaptive planning
finding: People overharvested on poor and neutral planets, not on rich ones. Overharvesting shrank with experience and grew after rare environment switches. A model with adaptive discounting under uncertainty explained it.
numbers: 116 analysed of 176 (60 excluded). Overharvest overall t(115)=3.88, P=.00018. After rare switch t(115)=4.67, P<.0001. Cross-validation (lower better): adaptive discounting 16.55 (best for 64%), TD 22.47 (14%), MVT learning 32.31 (22%; predicted underharvesting, t=-7.26).
quote: overharvesting is a consequence of optimal learning and adaptation
limits: Online MTurk sample, 34% excluded. No effect size in text.
agent_relevance: Overstaying may be rational when the environment is uncertain. Do not simply force early leaving; first check whether the environment is stable.

source: Guldener et al. (2024) Differential patch-leaving behavior during probabilistic foraging in humans and gerbils
finding: Some humans overstayed (long giving-up time) and earned less; gerbils did not. Both species showed MVT-like sensitivity to collection rate.
numbers: 42 humans analysed of 52; 18 gerbils (9 long-GUT, 9 short-GUT). Mean rate 0.165 rewards/s. Human GUT about 10.4 s vs 4.1 s; residence about 50 s vs 30 s. Residence vs earnings r=-0.717 (lab) and -0.653 (fMRI); none in gerbils. Cox hazard ratio per reward 0.20 (short GUT), 0.27 (long GUT), 0.06 (gerbils).
limits: Long-GUT humans not MVT-optimal. Median split at 6.951 s is post hoc.
agent_relevance: Overstaying has a cost that scales with stay length. Threshold differs between individuals (here, between models); calibrate per task family.

source: Stochastic choice drives variability in patch foraging decisions in humans and rats (2026)
finding: Variability in leaving time is explained by a fixed stochastic choice process, not by learning noise. Most subjects had a reward-independent bias toward leaving.
numbers: Reanalysis of 3 datasets: field-human N=39, berry-human N=29, rat N=8. Early vs late variability field t(38)=0.98, berry t(28)=0.85, rat W(7)=22; Bayes factors 3.71, 3.64, 2.55 for no change. Parameter recovery r>=0.87. SD of leaving time 1-5 s, 20-50% of the mean.
limits: Reanalysis, not preregistered. Deviation size in figures only.
agent_relevance: A code-applied threshold plus noise is realistic. Do not expect exact-optimal leaving; test across seeds.

source: Social information foraging in macaques follows the Marginal Value Theorem (Sci Rep 2017)
finding: Monkeys stayed longer on face-patches when travel was longer; an MVT model with value and time terms fit best.
numbers: 3 male macaques. Patch-leaving decisions: color valence 3187, fractal 3945, social vs nonsocial 2142. Kendall tau 0.069, 0.079, 0.075 (all P<0.0001). Two of three monkeys not significant in social/nonsocial (P=0.056, 0.058). Akaike weights 0.828-0.979.
limits: Tiny N; MVT simulation overestimated residence time; effects small (tau about 0.07). Authors name is not in the page text read.
agent_relevance: MVT logic extends beyond food to information, but effects can be small.

source: Webb et al. (2025) Foraging animals use dynamic Bayesian updating to model meta-uncertainty
finding: Mouse leaving times were best fit by a hierarchical Bayesian model that updates its belief about the decay rate. Simple heuristics and optimal MVT fit worse.
numbers: 8 freely moving mice, 17,877 patches (385 sessions; discussion says 14,060/300). RMSE low stochasticity: constant time 4.88, MVT-OPT 4.90, MVT-IM 4.10, best Bayesian MAP-IM-GL 3.54. Decay rate vs residence r=0.50. Head-fixed 3 mice, 2,086 patches.
quote: mice forage under meta-uncertainty by employing a hierarchical Bayesian strategy
limits: Mice only; inconsistent patch counts in the paper; MAP-IM-L gain over MVT-IM not significant.
agent_relevance: Estimating how fast an operator's yield falls beats a fixed rule.

source: Charnov (1976) Optimal foraging, the marginal value theorem
finding: Founding theory: a forager in a patchy environment should leave a patch when its instantaneous intake rate falls to the long-term average rate for the whole habitat, including travel time.
numbers: Rule: leave when g'(t) equals g(t*)/(t*+travel). Longer travel means longer stay (concave gain curve).
limits: Not opened; stated from standard knowledge. Assumes known gain curve, no uncertainty, rate maximising.
agent_relevance: The core S6 rule: leave an operator when its current yield drops below the average yield of the whole run.

source: Stephens and Krebs (1986) Foraging Theory
finding: Textbook account of patch models, prey models, information and risk-sensitivity extensions, and the tests that followed.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source for extensions (uncertainty, variance) that matter when yield is noisy.

source: Charnov and Orians (1973) Optimal foraging: some theoretical explorations
finding: Earlier formulation of optimal patch use that Charnov (1976) formalised as the marginal value theorem.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; citation only.
agent_relevance: Historical backing.

source: Hutchinson, Wilke, Todd (2008) Patch leaving in humans: can a generalist adapt its rules to dispersal of items across patches?
finding: Human visual foragers adapted their patch-leaving rule to item dispersal, using simple rules such as giving-up time rather than exact MVT.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; from memory of the abstract.
agent_relevance: Simple stopping rules (giving-up time, fixed count) are the competitors to the MVT rule.

source: Wolfe (2013) When is it time to move to the next raspberry bush? Foraging rules in human visual search
finding: Humans in visual search leave a patch roughly when the current rate falls to the overall average, as MVT predicts, with variation.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; from memory.
agent_relevance: Support that humans apply an average-rate rule in cognitive tasks, not only for food.

source: Hills, Jones, Todd (2012) Optimal foraging in semantic memory
finding: In verbal fluency, people moved between semantic clusters when within-cluster retrieval rate fell below the global average, as MVT predicts.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; from memory.
agent_relevance: Closest link from foraging to thinking: mental search among ideas follows the same leave rule. Supports using it for operator switching.

source: Search for LLM or AI studies testing the MVT leave rule (this agent's attempt)
finding: No LLM study that directly tests or applies the marginal value theorem was found. The web search quota was exhausted and API lookups were rate limited, so this is a gap in the search, not proof of absence.
numbers: Europe PMC query for patch foraging/MVT with language model or LLM returned 7 items; none was a direct test (closest: 2026 semantic fluency network papers and a spontaneous-thought foraging preprint, not opened).
limits: Search incomplete.
agent_relevance: A later run should look for LLM work on stopping, overthinking and search budget.

source: Spontaneous thought transitions follow a foraging-like policy on high-order memory patches (bioRxiv 2026 preprint)
finding: Title says thought transitions follow a foraging-like policy. Details not read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Title only, from a database listing.
agent_relevance: Possible human evidence for foraging rules in internal thought.

source: Webb et al. (2025) heuristics versus MVT in mice
finding: Simple heuristics (constant time, count of rewards, time since last reward) were compared with MVT variants. Number-of-rewards rule fit worst; constant time was about as good as optimal MVT.
numbers: Low stochasticity RMSE: constant time 4.88, time since reward 5.86, number of rewards 6.57, MVT-OPT 4.90. High stochasticity: 4.92, 4.67, 7.03, 4.85.
limits: Mice, one lab, travel and decay manipulated by track length.
agent_relevance: A fixed budget per operator is a strong baseline; a yield-based rule must beat it to be worth adding. Counting attempts alone is worst.
